oneSentence: A machine learning method that sorts an input into one of several named categories based on patterns learned from examples.
plainExplanation:
Classification is used when you want a system to choose a category from a fixed set. For example, an email might be labelled “spam” or “not spam”, or a document might be labelled “invoice”, “contract” or “report”. The input can be text, an image, a sound clip or a row of numbers.

During training, the system is shown many examples along with the correct category. Those correct categories are called labels. From these examples, it adjusts internal settings so that certain patterns in the input become linked with certain labels.

Later, during inference, a new input goes in. The system turns that input into measurable signals, often called features, such as words present in a message or shapes in an image. It then produces a prediction: which class seems most likely, sometimes with a score for each class.

Classification is different from regression, which predicts a number such as temperature or price. It is also different from clustering, which groups similar items without using pre-named categories. In classification, the categories are defined in advance, even if the model sometimes gets them wrong.

everydayAnalogy.title: Tuning a radio to label a station
everydayAnalogy.story: Aisha is driving from Nairobi to Arusha and turns the radio dial to find a clear station. At each frequency, she listens for clues: spoken news, music style, language and signal quality. She then marks the station on a list as “news”, “music” or “talk”, based on what best matches what she hears. If the signal is weak, she may still choose a label, but with less confidence.

clues like language, voice and music style

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A person tuning a radio can use broad real-world knowledge and can change the categories if needed. A classifier usually works only with the classes it was trained for, and its internal matching process is mathematical rather than conscious listening. Also, many classifiers output scores for all classes at once, not a person-like step-by-step judgement.

visual.title: How classification turns an input into a category
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, the reader should be able to say that classification takes an input, measures useful features, compares learned patterns and outputs one named class.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. It shows a new input entering the system, being converted into features, compared with patterns learned during training, and ending with a class prediction and confidence scores. Read from left to right.

steps.label: 1. New input arrives
steps.explanation: A text, image, sound clip or data record is presented to the model for sorting.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box on the left labelled “Input” with small icons for a document, photo and waveform. Add a caption: “Example: message, image or form entry”.

steps.label: 2. Signals are measured
steps.explanation: The system represents parts of the input as features, such as words, shapes, colours or numeric values.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box labelled “Features” containing tokens like “urgent”, “invoice”, a small shape outline and bars for numeric values.

steps.label: 3. Learned patterns are compared
steps.explanation: The model uses patterns learned from labelled examples to estimate how strongly the input matches each class.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box labelled “Model” with three horizontal score bars named Class A, Class B and Class C, each at different lengths.

steps.label: 4. A class is returned
steps.explanation: The output is a prediction, often the highest-scoring class, sometimes alongside confidence-like scores.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box labelled “Prediction” with one highlighted result such as “Invoice” and smaller secondary scores beneath it.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each box reveals one concrete example for text, image and tabular data; arrows highlight in sequence from input to prediction.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow from left to right. First, a new input enters, such as a message, image or form entry. Second, the system measures features from that input, like words, shapes or numbers. Third, the model compares those features with patterns learned earlier from labelled examples and produces scores for each possible class. Fourth, it returns the class with the strongest score, for example labelling a document as an invoice. The main lesson is that classification outputs a named category, not an open-ended answer or a numeric estimate.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right diagram with four labelled boxes: Input, Features, Model and Prediction. Short example text under each box replaces any animated highlighting.

workedExample.scenario: Sorting support emails for a small health clinic
workedExample.input: Email text: “Hello, I need to move my appointment from Tuesday to Friday if possible.”
process: The system receives the email text as input.
It measures features such as words and phrases like “move”, “appointment”, “Tuesday” and “Friday”.
The classifier compares these features with patterns learned from labelled emails in classes such as “appointment change”, “billing question” and “medical records request”.
It assigns scores: appointment change 0.91, billing question 0.06, medical records request 0.03.
It outputs the top class as the prediction.
workedExample.result: Predicted class: “appointment change”. A staff member can then route the email to the scheduling team.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN procurement team is drafting requirements for software that automatically sorts incoming vendor questions into categories such as technical clarification, submission issue or contract terms question.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Understanding classification helps staff ask the right questions: what classes are predefined, how labels were created, how accuracy will be tested, and how errors such as misrouting will be handled with human oversight.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not test public AI services with confidential procurement documents, bidder information or any commercially sensitive material unless the service is approved for that use.

whyItMatters: Classification affects how information is routed, filtered and prioritised. A system may flag content as risky, sort messages into queues, or label documents for faster handling. If you understand classification, you can ask practical questions: What are the classes? Who chose the labels? How often does it confuse one class with another? What happens when it is unsure? These questions matter because errors have consequences. A false alarm can waste time or unfairly block something. A missed case can hide an urgent issue. Non-specialists do not need to build classifiers, but they often need to judge whether one is suitable, what data it needs and where human review is still necessary.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Classification always gives a yes-or-no answer.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Some classifiers are binary, with two classes such as approved or rejected, but many choose among three or more classes. A system can also return a score for each class, not just a single hard label.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the model is 90% confident, it is correct 90% of the time for every case.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A score is not automatically a trustworthy probability. Some models are poorly calibrated, meaning their confidence-like numbers do not match real-world accuracy. Performance can also differ across classes and contexts.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Classification finds natural groups in data by itself.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That describes clustering more than classification. In classification, the categories are named in advance and the system learns from examples linked to those labels.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Classification is teaching a system to put each new item into one of a set of named buckets, like sorting messages into “spam” or “not spam”.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In machine learning, classification is a supervised learning task that maps an input x to one label from a finite set of classes. A model is trained on labelled examples to learn a decision function or class probability estimate based on features in the input. At inference time, it computes scores for the possible classes and returns the highest-scoring class, or multiple class scores, depending on the design. Common variants include binary classification, multiclass classification and multilabel classification, where one item can receive more than one label. Evaluation often examines per-class performance, confusion between classes and trade-offs such as false positives versus false negatives.

keyTakeaway: Classification predicts which named category an input belongs to, using patterns learned from labelled examples.

quickCheck.question: Which situation is a classification task?
options: Grouping unlabeled photos by visual similarity
Writing a summary of a meeting note
quickCheck.explanation: Classification chooses from predefined categories. “Urgent”, “routine” and “irrelevant” are named classes decided in advance. Predicting rainfall is regression, grouping unlabeled photos is clustering, and writing a summary is a text generation task.
